children: Shares of on-demand food delivery service DoorDash
jumped 5.6% in the morning session after the company agreed to acquire Instacart for approximately $17 billion and reported record third-quarter financial results.

According to the company's announcement, DoorDash reached a definitive agreement to acquire Instacart for $65.00 per share, representing an equity value of approximately $17 billion. The transaction consideration will be payable in at least 75% cash and up to 25% DoorDash stock. Concurrently, DoorDash announced financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, achieving new quarterly records across Marketplace GOV, revenue, and net income. DoorDash announced better-than-expected revenue in Q3 2026, with sales up 34% year on year to $4.62 billion. Its GAAP profit of $1.06 per share was 31.4% above analysts’ consensus estimates.
The major acquisition significantly expands DoorDash's presence in online grocery delivery, while its record financial results reinforce investor confidence in continued operational strength.
What is the market telling us

DoorDash’s shares are quite volatile and have had 18 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 15 days ago when the stock dropped 5.9% on the news that the major indices pulled back and tech-oriented equities fell as the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a hotter-than-expected September inflation print, pushing Treasury yields higher.

As detailed by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the consumer price index rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, topping the 3.6% estimate from economists polled by Dow Jones. According to CNBC, core inflation—which excludes volatile food and energy costs—climbed 2.6% annually against expectations of 2.5%. Following the print, CNBC market data showed the 10-year Treasury yield climbed over six basis points to 5.278%, while the 30-year yield advanced past 5.59%. According to market commentators, rising yields intensify pressure on equity valuations as third-quarter corporate earnings get underway. In remarks carried by CNBC, Franklin Templeton Institute head investment strategist Jeff Schulze noted that pressure across the long end of the curve acts as a severe valuation headwind for risk assets.

Financial analysts explain that higher benchmark yields mechanically elevate the discount rate applied to corporate earnings, compressing the multiples investors are willing to pay for equities. Ultimately, CNBC noted that when sticky inflation dampens expectations for monetary easing, the repricing falls heaviest on high-multiple growth and gig-economy sectors whose projected cash flows sit furthest in the future.

DoorDash is down 17.5% since the beginning of the year, and at $181.41 per share, it is trading 31.8% below its 52-week high of $266.06 from October 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of DoorDash’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $931.28.
